name: Database Internals
description: Storage engines, B-trees vs LSM, WAL, MVCC, locking and how a query planner decides what to do.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Database Internals is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is a database management system (DBMS)?
cards.answer: The software that stores data durably and lets many clients query and change it safely at the same time — handling storage on disk, indexes, query planning, transactions, concurrency and crash recovery.
cards.explanation: PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite are DBMSs. "Database internals" is the study of how they do this; knowing it explains why some queries are fast, others slow, and why the database occasionally needs maintenance.

cards.prompt: What is a database index?
cards.answer: A separate data structure (usually a B-tree) that keeps a column's values sorted with pointers to their rows, so the database can find matching rows without scanning the whole table — like the index at the back of a book.
cards.explanation: Indexes make reads on the indexed columns dramatically faster but cost disk space and slow down every insert and update, which must keep the index current. Index the columns you filter and join on.

cards.prompt: What is a transaction?
cards.answer: A group of database operations that succeed or fail as one unit. A bank transfer debits one account and credits another; a transaction guarantees you never end up with only half of it done.
cards.explanation: You `BEGIN` a transaction, make changes, then `COMMIT` to keep them or `ROLLBACK` to undo them all. The guarantees transactions provide are summarised as ACID.

cards.prompt: What does ACID stand for, in one line each?
cards.answer: Atomicity: all of a transaction happens or none of it. Consistency: it leaves the data valid under all rules. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work. Durability: once committed, it survives a crash.
cards.explanation: Durability is usually achieved with a write-ahead log (WAL): changes are recorded in a log on disk before being applied, so after a crash the database can replay or undo them.

cards.prompt: How does a database store data on disk, at a high level?
cards.answer: In fixed-size pages (often 4–16 KB) inside data files. Tables and indexes are made of pages, a buffer pool caches hot pages in RAM, and a log records every change for crash recovery.
cards.explanation: Reading one row still loads its whole page, which is why related data stored close together (and sequential scans) can be faster than many random lookups.

cards.prompt: What is a query planner (optimiser)?
cards.answer: The database component that decides how to execute a SQL query — which indexes to use, the order to join tables, which join algorithm — by estimating the cost of alternative plans from table statistics.
cards.explanation: Because SQL is declarative, the same query can be run many ways and the planner picks one. `EXPLAIN` shows you the chosen plan, which is the first tool for diagnosing a slow query.

modules.name: Storage & Durability
modules.description: How rows reach disk and survive a crash.

cards.prompt: What is a write-ahead log, and why does it make commits fast *and* durable?
cards.answer: Changes are appended to a sequential log and fsync-ed before the data pages are updated. A commit only needs one sequential write; the random page writes happen later at a checkpoint. On crash, the log is replayed.
cards.explanation: Sequential fsync is orders of magnitude cheaper than random writes across the heap. The WAL also powers replication (ship the log), point-in-time recovery and, in Postgres, the visibility bookkeeping MVCC needs.

cards.prompt: B-tree vs LSM-tree storage engines
cards.answer: B-trees update pages in place — read-optimised; LSM-trees append to sorted files and merge later — write-optimised.

left.title: B-tree (Postgres, InnoDB)
points: Write amplification from page splits and WAL

right.title: LSM (RocksDB, Cassandra)
points: Sequential writes into memtable then SSTables
Reads may touch several levels — Bloom filters help
Background compaction costs I/O and can spike latency

cards.explanation: Pick by workload shape: write-heavy ingestion and time-series suit LSM; mixed OLTP with lots of point reads and range scans suits B-trees. Both amplify writes, just at different times — B-trees now, LSM during compaction.

cards.prompt: How does MVCC let readers avoid blocking writers?
cards.answer: Each write creates a new row version tagged with transaction IDs. A reader sees the snapshot of versions visible to its own transaction, so it never waits on a writer's lock.
cards.explanation: The cost is garbage: dead versions must be reclaimed (Postgres VACUUM, InnoDB purge). A long-running transaction pins old versions and causes table bloat — which is why an idle-in-transaction connection can quietly degrade the whole database.

cards.prompt: What is the buffer pool, and why is its hit rate the first metric you check?
cards.answer: An in-memory cache of disk pages. If the working set fits, most reads never touch storage; once it does not, every miss becomes an I/O and latency changes by orders of magnitude.
cards.explanation: A hit rate falling off a cliff usually means the data outgrew RAM or a query started scanning something huge and evicted everything useful. Sizing (`shared_buffers`, `innodb_buffer_pool_size`) is the highest-leverage tuning knob there is.

modules.name: Locking & Query Execution
modules.description: Locks, deadlocks, join strategies and how the planner chooses.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between shared and exclusive locks, and what is a row lock versus a table lock?
cards.answer: Shared (read) locks are compatible with each other; exclusive (write) locks are compatible with nothing. Row locks affect single rows; table locks affect everything and are usually taken by DDL.
cards.explanation: Most OLTP contention comes from unexpected escalation or from DDL: an `ALTER TABLE` needing an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock will queue behind long readers and then block every new query behind it. Always set a `lock_timeout` for migrations.

cards.prompt: Two transactions update the same two rows in opposite order and one is aborted. What happened, and how do you prevent it?
cards.answer: A deadlock: each holds a lock the other needs, and the detector kills the cheaper victim. Prevent it by always updating rows in a consistent order (for example, ascending primary key) and keeping transactions short.
cards.explanation: Databases detect rather than prevent deadlocks, so your application must be able to retry the aborted transaction. That retry path deserves a test — it is exercised rarely and is a common source of data corruption when written carelessly.

cards.prompt: What are the three main join algorithms, and when does the planner pick each?
cards.answer: Nested loop (small outer input, indexed inner), hash join (large unsorted inputs, equality predicates), merge join (both inputs already sorted, or sortable cheaply — also handles range joins).
cards.explanation: Seeing a nested loop over millions of rows in a plan almost always means the planner underestimated cardinality. Fix the statistics or the predicate rather than forcing a join type — hints, where they exist, freeze a decision that should stay adaptive.

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — Join operations

cards.prompt: Your app opens 500 database connections and throughput collapses. Why, and what is the fix?
cards.answer: Each Postgres connection is a process with its own memory; hundreds of them thrash CPU and memory while only a few can make progress. Use a connection pool (PgBouncer, HikariCP) sized near the core count plus disk parallelism.
cards.explanation: The counter-intuitive result is that fewer connections give higher throughput and lower latency — the queue moves to the pool, where it is cheap, instead of the database, where it is not. Serverless platforms need a proxy for exactly this reason.

cards.prompt: How do you add a NOT NULL column to a 500-million-row table without downtime?
cards.answer: In steps: add the column as nullable (metadata-only on modern versions), backfill in batches, add a NOT VALID check constraint, validate it concurrently, then set NOT NULL. Deploy code that tolerates both shapes first.
cards.explanation: This is the expand–migrate–contract pattern: never change schema and code in one irreversible step. Create indexes with CONCURRENTLY, batch backfills to avoid long transactions and lock queues, and always set a lock timeout.

modules.name: Replication, Recovery & Scaling
modules.description: Query planning and statistics, vacuum, replication, backups and PITR, partitioning, sharding and CDC.

cards.prompt: How does a cost-based query planner choose a plan, and why does it sometimes choose badly?
cards.answer: It enumerates candidate plans (scan types, join orders, join algorithms), estimates each one's cost from table statistics — row counts, value distributions, correlations — and picks the cheapest estimate. Bad choices almost always trace back to bad row-count estimates.
cards.explanation: Stale statistics after bulk loads, correlated columns the planner assumes independent, and parameters with skewed distributions are the usual causes. Fix with `ANALYZE`, extended statistics (`CREATE STATISTICS`), or rewriting the query — before reaching for hints.

cards.prompt: A Postgres table's size keeps growing although the row count is stable, and queries slow down. What is happening?
cards.answer: Bloat: every UPDATE and DELETE leaves dead tuples under MVCC, and autovacuum is not reclaiming them fast enough — often because a long-running or idle-in-transaction session holds back the oldest visible snapshot. Find and end that session, and tune autovacuum for the hot table.
cards.explanation: Plain VACUUM makes dead space reusable but rarely shrinks the file; `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table under an exclusive lock (pg_repack does it online). Vacuum also prevents transaction-ID wraparound, which is why it must never be disabled.

cards.prompt: Physical (streaming) replication vs logical replication
cards.answer: Physical replication ships the WAL byte-for-byte, producing an exact copy of the whole cluster; logical replication decodes changes into row-level operations for selected tables, which the subscriber applies.
cards.explanation: Physical replicas are for high availability and read scaling, and must run the same major version. Logical replication enables zero-downtime major-version upgrades, selective replication and feeding other systems — but does not replicate schema changes (DDL) automatically.

cards.prompt: Someone ran `DELETE FROM customers` without a WHERE clause at 14:03. How do you recover, and what must already be in place?
cards.answer: Point-in-time recovery: restore the last base backup and replay archived WAL up to 14:02:59, into a separate instance, then copy the lost rows back. It requires continuous WAL archiving plus regular base backups — set up before the incident.
cards.explanation: A backup is only real once a restore has been tested — schedule restore drills and measure how long they take (your real RTO). Replicas are not backups: the DELETE replicates to them within milliseconds. Delayed replicas give a short grace window.

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs — Continuous archiving and point-in-time recovery

cards.prompt: What does table partitioning buy you within a single database?
cards.answer: Partition pruning (queries touching one time range scan only its partitions), cheap retention (drop an old partition instead of deleting millions of rows), and smaller per-partition indexes and vacuum work.
cards.explanation: Choose the partition key from the dominant filter — usually time for events and logs. Partitioning does not add capacity beyond one machine; that is sharding. Too many partitions add planning overhead, so avoid thousands of tiny ones.

cards.prompt: Your primary database is at the limit of the largest instance available. What are the options before and when sharding?
cards.answer: Before: optimise queries and indexes, add read replicas for read traffic, cache, archive cold data, and move independent domains to separate databases. Sharding — splitting rows across databases by a shard key such as tenant ID — comes last.
cards.explanation: Sharding makes cross-shard joins, transactions, unique constraints and rebalancing hard, and the key is very expensive to change. Tenant-based keys fit SaaS well because most queries stay within one tenant. Distributed SQL systems (Citus, CockroachDB, Spanner) absorb some of this complexity.

resources.title: Citus docs — Choosing a distribution column

cards.prompt: A service must update its database and publish an event. How do you avoid the event being lost if the process crashes between the two?
cards.answer: The transactional outbox: write the event into an `outbox` table in the same transaction as the data change, then a relay — polling, or change-data-capture reading the WAL (Debezium) — publishes it to the broker. Publish at least once and make consumers idempotent.
cards.explanation: Writing to the database and a broker are two systems with no shared transaction (the dual-write problem): either order can leave one without the other. The outbox turns it into one local transaction plus reliable, retryable delivery.
